lesson.title: Launching the War on Terror
lesson.summary: In response to the September 11 attacks, the George W. Bush administration declared a global war on terrorism, invading Afghanistan to remove the Taliban and al Qaeda and reshaping American military and security policy for a generation.
lesson.body:
Nine days after the September 11 attacks, President George W. Bush addressed a joint session of Congress and declared what he called a war on terror, vowing to pursue not only the perpetrators of the attacks but any government that harbored terrorists. Congress quickly passed an Authorization for Use of Military Force, granting the president broad power to act against those responsible for 9/11 and those who had aided them, a legal foundation that would be cited to justify American military operations for the next two decades.

The first target was Afghanistan, whose ruling Taliban government had given al Qaeda and Osama bin Laden safe haven to plan the attacks. On October 7, 2001, the United States and coalition allies launched Operation Enduring Freedom, combining air strikes with support for Afghan opposition forces on the ground. The Taliban government fell within weeks, though bin Laden escaped into the mountainous border region with Pakistan, and Afghanistan itself would remain a site of ongoing conflict for years afterward, eventually becoming the longest war in American history.

The War on Terror quickly expanded beyond Afghanistan into a broader global campaign against terrorist organizations and the states seen as supporting them. In his January 2002 State of the Union address, Bush labeled Iraq, Iran, and North Korea an axis of evil, language that signaled a much wider set of ambitions than simply hunting down al Qaeda and laid rhetorical groundwork for the invasion of Iraq the following year. The administration also built new institutions and tools for the fight, including a detention facility at the U.S. naval base at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, opened in January 2002 to hold terrorism suspects, often without traditional criminal trials, a practice that drew lasting international criticism over due process and the treatment of detainees.

At home, the War on Terror reshaped American government and daily life, from new airport security procedures to a reorganization of federal agencies. It also raised difficult, enduring questions about how a democracy balances the demand for security against its own founding commitments to civil liberties and the rule of law, questions that came into sharp focus with new surveillance laws passed in the immediate aftermath of the attacks.
